name: Tomato Fruit Blossom-End Rot
causal_agent: Calcium deficiency combined with irregular water uptake
symptoms: fruit: Dark, sunken lesion at blossom end of fruit Lesion may enlarge, become leathery, and lead to fruit rot First visible on young developing fruits, often in clusters Internal tissues may also be discolored if condition persists leaves_and_stems: No direct symptoms on leaves or stems; plants often appear healthy aboveground
management: cultural: Maintain even soil moisture during fruiting via controlled watering or drip irrigation Mulch to retain soil moisture and reduce fluctuations Provide adequate spacing and prune to ensure good air circulation and reduce relative humidity Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization; side-dress only if needed to maintain moderate growth Monitor plant vigor to ensure balance between root and shoot development chemical: Foliar application of calcium nitrate or calcium chloride (1.5 tsp per gallon water + 0.5 tsp surfactant, e.g., CapSil) weekly during fruiting Apply sprays in the early morning to reduce risk of phytotoxicity Avoid excessive calcium applications as it may reduce yields or cause foliage injury preventive_notes: Focus on consistent cultural practices and calcium availability rather than relying solely on foliar sprays Monitor soil calcium levels prior to planting and amend soils if needed
sources: Brubaker, V. 2016. Calcium: It does a plant good. Greenhouse Grower, January.
